thread.title: Frank 'Bucko' Kilroy remembered for toughness and impact on Philadelphia Eagles history
thread.title_full: Frank 'Bucko' Kilroy remembered for toughness and impact on Philadelphia Eagles history

author: philly leader
title: Frank 'Bucko' Kilroy remembered for toughness and impact on Philadelphia Eagles history
text:
Ray Didinger, a former NFL Films producer, reflected on the legacy of Frank “Bucko” Kilroy and his role with the Philadelphia Eagles’ championship teams of 1948 and 1949. The Eagles, under coach Earle (Greasy) Neale, achieved a combined record of 20-3-1 during those two seasons and won both title games by shutout.
The team’s success was attributed to a strong defense that used innovative tactics for its time. Notable players included Steve Van Buren, Pete Pihos, Tommy Thompson, Chuck Bednarik, and Alex Wojciechowicz—all later inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame. Despite these stars, Kilroy’s name frequently surfaced in interviews with former teammates.
“We intimidated a lot of teams,” halfback Russ Craft said. “We intimidated them with our talent and Bucko intimidated them by just walking on the field. He intimidated me and I was on his team.”
Kilroy joined the Eagles in 1943 as a free agent from Northeast Catholic High School and Temple University. Recalling his signing, Kilroy said: “The day they signed me, Greasy took me to the basement of the Eagles’ offices…He said, ‘I know your kind. You make just one false move and I’ll kick you right off the team on your fat Irish haunches.’ Only he didn’t say haunches.”
Throughout his 13-season career with Philadelphia as a two-way lineman, Kilroy earned All-Pro honors from 1948 through 1954 and was named to the NFL’s All-Decade Team for the 1940s.
“Bucko was so big and naturally strong, people just couldn’t handle him,” Craft recalled in a 1999 interview. “He’d put those two big paws out there and he’d stop anything that came his way and if they were a little afraid of him besides…that just added to his advantage.”
A Chicago sportswriter once described Kilroy as “a knuckle-duster in knee pants who gives our fellows that boyish grin while kicking their teeth loose in a pileup.” Didinger’s review of archival footage confirmed Kilroy’s reputation as an enforcer.
“I played to the whistle,” Kilroy stated. “And back then they didn’t blow the whistles as fast as they do today.”
Teammate Steve Van Buren noted: “Bucko knew what he was doing…Sometimes he’d do stuff just to make them mad. They’d take a swing at Bucko and get tossed out of the game.”
Kilroy became nationally known after Life Magazine focused on him in its story about violence in pro football titled “Savagery on Sunday.” When then-NFL Commissioner Bert Bell sued Life Magazine for slander over its portrayal of Kilroy—and won—the jury awarded $11,600 in damages to Kilroy.
“After that,” said Kilroy, “if anyone ever accused me of being a dirty player, I could say, ‘I was acquitted by a jury,’ which I was.”
After serving as player-coach with Philadelphia in 1955 before moving fully into coaching roles—including work with Dallas Cowboys—Kilroy eventually joined New England Patriots management until retiring in 2006. His professional football career spanned more than six decades.
Reflecting on changes within professional football over time during an interview with Didinger in 1999, Kilroy observed: “There is so much money now and…free agency…You don’t have the same loyalty…(Players) now are more loyal to themselves than they are to their teams…In our day it was like one big fraternity. We played because we loved the game…”
